scams.name: Taxi Meter Manipulation
scams.description:
You arrive at Antalya Airport and head toward the taxi rank. A driver in the arrivals hall approaches before you reach the licensed stand outside and offers a "fixed price" to your hotel, quoting in euros rather than Turkish lira.

The metered fare from the airport to the city center runs 150–250 TL on the day rate. The driver's euro quote converts to nearly double that at his own exchange rate. Other drivers run the meter on the night rate (Tarife 2) during daylight hours, or take circuitous routes through empty streets to inflate the distance. Drivers approaching inside the terminal often operate personal vehicles with unofficial taxi markings.

Walk past drivers inside the terminal to the official licensed taxi stand outside arrivals, say "sayaç açın" (start the meter) before boarding, and monitor it throughout the trip. Use the BiTaksi app for app-regulated fares with digital receipts. If a driver quotes in euros, ask for the lira equivalent and compare with the metered rate.
scams.avoidance: Always insist the meter is running and set to the daytime rate (gunduz tarife) before the car moves Use the BiTaksi app to book taxis with tracked routes and pre-estimated fares, or arrange a hotel transfer in advance At Antalya Airport, use only the official taxi stand outside arrivals and reject drivers who approach you inside the terminal Know approximate fares: airport to Kaleici is roughly 350-500 TL, airport to Lara Beach is 250-400 TL in 2025 prices Request a receipt (makbuz) for every trip and report overcharging to local police at 155 or the tourism hotline
scams.location: Antalya Airport arrivals between Domestic and International terminals, Kaleici Old Town taxi stands, Lara Beach resort pickups, late-night rides from bars in the marina area
scams.tldr: Antalya taxi drivers refuse the meter, quote euros instead of lira at inflated exchange rates, or run the night rate during daytime — costing tourists $20–$80 more per ride than the metered fare on the same route.

scams.name: Restaurant Bill Inflation
scams.description:
A tout on the street in Kaleici or along the old harbor front invites you into a restaurant with photos of appealing food. The menu shows prices that seem fair. Bread and water arrive at the table without being ordered.

When the bill arrives, items are charged at two to three times their menu price. A fabricated "tax" line item adds 15–20%. The bread and water appear at 50–100 TL each. A service charge that was never mentioned adds another 15%. Staff resist correcting the discrepancies and pressure a quick payment.

Walk past any restaurant with a tout on the street — restaurants that need to recruit customers from the pavement charge 30–50% more than comparable establishments. Check each bill line-by-line against the menu before paying, and photograph the menu prices at the table. If items are billed above their menu price, point to the menu and pay the listed amount only.
scams.avoidance: Photograph the menu including prices before ordering, and compare each item to the bill before paying Avoid restaurants with aggressive touts on the street; choose places where locals eat and check Google reviews first Ask explicitly if bread, water, and service charges are included or extra before sitting down Always check the bill line by line and do not feel rushed; politely insist on time to review each charge If overcharged, refuse to pay the inflated amount and threaten to call the tourist police (155); restaurants often back down immediately
scams.location: Marina restaurants along Antalya harbor, Kaleici Old Town tourist restaurants, Lara Beach resort strip eateries, rooftop dining spots near Hadrian's Gate
scams.tldr: Restaurants along Antalya's tourist strips present reasonable menus but bill at two to three times the listed prices, adding fabricated "tax" lines, cover charges for unordered bread and water, and hidden 15% service charges never disclosed at seating.

scams.name: Carpet Shop Pressure Sales
scams.description:
You are walking through Kaleici when a friendly man approaches, invites you to see "authentic antique rugs," and leads you to a showroom. Tea arrives and the host begins unrolling carpets one by one, explaining the history and craft of each.

As the session extends to an hour or more, the emotional pressure builds: "I have shown you everything, you must take one home." Carpets labeled as handwoven Turkish silk are machine-made Chinese imports. Certificates of authenticity are printed in-house. Tourists report paying $2,000–$5,000 for pieces later appraised at $100–$300.

Do not enter any carpet shop you were recruited into from the street — legitimate dealers operate on referrals and do not employ pavement touts. If you want to buy a carpet in Turkey, visit only shops with consistent verified reviews on TripAdvisor or Google Maps, and ask for an independent appraisal before paying. Any certificate of authenticity should reference an independent testing body, not the seller.
scams.avoidance: Never follow a street tout into a carpet shop; if you want a carpet, research specific reputable dealers with verified reviews beforehand Get any carpet independently appraised before purchasing; do not rely on certificates provided by the seller Understand that feeling obligated after tea and conversation is the entire strategy; you owe nothing for accepting hospitality If you do buy, pay by credit card so you can dispute the charge if the carpet turns out to be fake or misrepresented Set a firm budget and a time limit before entering any shop, and do not let the salesperson talk you past either boundary
scams.location: Kaleici Old Town narrow streets, shops near Hadrian's Gate, tourist markets near the Clock Tower, carpet galleries along Ataturk Caddesi
scams.tldr: Touts in Kaleici invite tourists to carpet showrooms offering "125-year-old rugs," serve tea during hours-long sales sessions, and sell Chinese machine-made fakes as handwoven Turkish originals at $2,000–$5,000 — with certificates of authenticity printed in-house.

scams.name: Accommodation Booking Fraud
scams.description:
You find a beautiful villa in Kaleici or an apartment near Lara Beach listed at 30–50% below comparable properties on a social media group or unofficial rental site. The photos are professional, the host is responsive, and the deal appears genuine.

The host requests payment by bank transfer rather than through a booking platform, citing "lower fees." You transfer the deposit or full amount. On arrival, the address does not exist, the property is occupied by someone else, or the room is drastically inferior to the photos. Some legitimate hotels participate in a subtler variant: they accept your booking, then claim the reserved room is "unavailable" and offer a lower-category room with no price adjustment.

Book accommodation only through Booking.com, Airbnb, or a hotel's official website — never by bank transfer to a private social media listing. Confirmed bookings through legitimate platforms include cancellation and refund protections; bank transfers do not. If a "host" moves conversation off the booking platform before payment, treat it as a scam signal.
scams.avoidance: Book accommodation only through established platforms like Booking.com, Airbnb, or Hotels.com that offer verified listings and refund policies Never send money via bank transfer or Western Union for any accommodation booking Cross-reference the property address on Google Maps and Google Street View to verify it exists and matches the listing photos Read recent reviews specifically mentioning the property matching its description; look for multiple reviews across different months Contact the property directly using phone numbers found through independent searches, not just the number provided in the listing
scams.location: Online listings for Kaleici boutique hotels, Lara Beach apartment rentals, Belek golf resort area, Kemer coastal villas
scams.tldr: Fraudulent villa and apartment listings on social media and unofficial booking sites offer Antalya properties at 30–50% below market, request bank-transfer payment, then deliver non-existent addresses, occupied properties, or severely downgraded rooms.

scams.name: Watersport Equipment Bait and Switch
scams.description:
You book a jet ski ride on Konyaalti Beach advertised at $50–$80 for 15 minutes. The operator is friendly, the beach is busy, and the setup looks legitimate.

At the end of the ride, the operator demands a $30–$50 "fuel deposit" never mentioned upfront, or states the timer started at the safety briefing rather than when you entered the water. Parasailing operators collect full payment on shore, then end the ride early citing "wind conditions." After returning the equipment, operators sometimes point to pre-existing wear and demand $200–$500 in repair costs.

Confirm the total price including all deposits, insurance, and fuel charges in writing before any watersport session begins. Photograph any existing equipment damage before use and have the operator acknowledge its condition. Refuse any demands for repair costs for damage that was already present when you boarded.
scams.avoidance: Book watersports through your hotel or a licensed operator with posted prices and Google reviews rather than beach touts Get a written quote including all charges before committing, and confirm whether fuel, equipment, and insurance are included Pay by credit card when possible for dispute protection; if paying cash, insist on a receipt with the business name and total Photograph any equipment before use so you have evidence against fake damage claims Check that the operator has a Turkish tourism license displayed and carries third-party liability insurance
scams.location: Konyaalti Beach, Lara Beach public area, Kemer resort beaches, Belek coastal strip
scams.tldr: Jet ski and parasailing operators on Konyaalti Beach quote a low entry price then add mandatory "fuel deposits," insurance fees, or photo charges mid-session — and sometimes claim post-ride damage to extract $200–$500 in fabricated repair costs.

scams.name: Bar Drink Spiking and Bill Inflation
scams.description:
You are near Kaleici late in the evening when an attractive person strikes up a friendly conversation and suggests a "nice bar nearby." The bar looks legitimate, the first drinks arrive quickly, and the prices quoted seem ordinary.

At the end of the night, the bill is $500–$2,000 for a few rounds. When you protest, bouncers block the exit. Entrance fees and per-drink "soft drink fees" appear as line items that were never disclosed. In the more dangerous variant, a sedative is added to a drink — victims wake hours later with phones, wallets, and watches stolen, and no memory of the intervening period.

Never follow a stranger's bar recommendation in Kaleici at night — choose your venue independently from a place with published drink prices and regular tourist foot traffic. Never leave a drink unattended or accept one from a new acquaintance. If confronted by bouncers over a fabricated bill, call Tourism Police on 155 before paying anything.
scams.avoidance: Never go to a bar suggested by a stranger you just met; choose your own venue based on Google reviews and visible foot traffic Always check the menu with prices before ordering and keep it at your table for reference when the bill arrives Never leave your drink unattended; order bottled drinks and open them yourself when possible Set a spending limit and pay for each round as it arrives rather than running a tab Go out in groups rather than alone, and let someone know where you are going and when you expect to return
scams.location: Bar Street (Barlar Sokagi) in Kaleici, clubs near the marina, late-night bars in Lara Beach hotel zone, rooftop bars targeting solo male tourists
scams.tldr: An attractive "local" steers tourists to a Kaleici bar that is in on the scam — drinks that seemed reasonably priced produce a bill of $500–$2,000 backed by bouncers at the door, and the more dangerous variant involves drink spiking followed by robbery of phones, wallets, and watches.
